entries.answer: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the field of computer science that builds systems able to perform tasks that normally need human intelligence, such as learning, reasoning, problem solving, understanding language and perceiving the world.
Machine Learning (ML) is a branch of AI where algorithms learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed. The three main types are supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning.

Deep Learning uses neural networks with many layers to learn complex patterns automatically. It powers modern image recognition, speech recognition and language models, and usually needs a lot of data and computing power (GPUs).

An artificial neural network is a model inspired by the brain: layers of connected 'neurons' that apply weights and an activation function to their inputs. Networks are trained with backpropagation and gradient descent, which adjust the weights to reduce prediction error.

Supervised learning trains a model on labeled examples (input and the correct output). It is used for classification (spam or not spam) and regression (predicting a price). Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression and decision trees are common algorithms.
Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data, for example grouping similar customers (clustering) or compressing features (dimensionality reduction such as PCA).

In reinforcement learning an agent learns by interacting with an environment: it takes actions, receives rewards or penalties, and improves its policy to maximise long-term reward. It is used in game playing and robotics.
Natural Language Processing (NLP) lets computers understand, interpret and generate human language. Typical tasks are tokenization, sentiment analysis, translation, question answering and chatbots.

Computer Vision enables machines to interpret images and video: image classification, object detection, face recognition and medical imaging. Most modern systems use convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

A chatbot is a program that holds a conversation with users in text or voice. Rule-based chatbots (like me) match patterns and return predefined replies; AI-based chatbots use machine learning or language models to generate their answers.

A rule-based system makes decisions using hand-written IF-THEN rules instead of learning from data. It is transparent and predictable, but it cannot handle situations its rules do not cover. Expert systems and rule-based chatbots are examples.

An expert system imitates a human expert in a narrow domain. It has a knowledge base of facts and rules plus an inference engine that applies them (forward or backward chaining). MYCIN, an early medical diagnosis system, is a classic example.

In a chatbot, pattern matching compares the user's text with patterns, often regular expressions, to detect an intent such as greeting or help, and then returns the linked response. That is exactly how I decide what you mean.
An intent is the goal behind a user's message, for example 'greeting', 'help' or 'goodbye'. A chatbot detects the intent first and then chooses a suitable response.

Proposed by Alan Turing in 1950, the Turing Test asks whether a machine can converse so well that a human judge cannot reliably tell it from a person. It is a famous benchmark idea for machine intelligence.

AI search algorithms explore a state space to find a path to a goal. Uninformed methods (BFS, DFS) use no extra knowledge; informed methods (greedy best-first, A*) use a heuristic to reach the goal faster.

Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores a graph level by level using a queue and finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph. Depth-First Search (DFS) follows one branch as deep as possible using a stack or recursion; it needs less memory but does not guarantee the shortest path.

A* is an informed search algorithm that finds the shortest path by always expanding the node with the lowest f(n) = g(n) + h(n), where g is the cost so far and h is a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost. It is optimal when the heuristic is admissible (never overestimates).

A heuristic is a rule of thumb that estimates how close a state is to the goal, for example Manhattan distance on a grid. Good heuristics make search much faster; an admissible heuristic never overestimates the true cost.

Classification is a supervised task that predicts a category for an input, such as spam or not spam, or positive or negative sentiment. Accuracy, precision, recall and the F1-score are common ways to evaluate it.

Regression predicts a continuous number, such as a house price or a temperature. Linear regression fits a straight line to the data. (Logistic regression, despite its name, is used for classification.)

Clustering is an unsupervised technique that groups similar data points without labels. K-means, the most popular algorithm, repeatedly assigns points to the nearest of k centroids and then moves each centroid to the mean of its points.

Overfitting happens when a model memorizes the training data, including its noise, and performs poorly on new data. Remedies: more data, simpler models, regularization, dropout, early stopping and cross-validation. Underfitting is the opposite: the model is too simple to capture the pattern.

Training data is the set of examples a model learns from. Data is normally split into a training set (to learn), a validation set (to tune settings) and a test set (to measure final performance on unseen data).

TF-IDF (Term Frequency - Inverse Document Frequency) turns text into numbers by weighting each word by how often it appears in a document and how rare it is across all documents. Words frequent in one document but rare overall get high scores.
Naive Bayes is a fast probabilistic classifier based on Bayes' theorem that assumes features are independent. It works surprisingly well on text tasks such as spam filtering and sentiment analysis.

Sentiment analysis is an NLP task that decides whether a text is positive, negative or neutral. It is used for product reviews, tweets and customer feedback, and can be done with word lists or with a classifier trained on TF-IDF features.

A Large Language Model (LLM) is a very large neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token. It can write, summarize, translate and answer questions, and it is the technology behind modern AI assistants.

The Transformer is a neural network architecture introduced in 2017 in the paper 'Attention Is All You Need'. Its self-attention mechanism lets the model weigh how relevant every word is to every other word, and it is the foundation of modern LLMs.
Generative AI creates new content such as text, images, audio, code or video by learning the patterns of existing data. Large language models and diffusion image generators are examples.

AI ethics covers fairness, bias, privacy, transparency and accountability. Models can inherit bias from their training data, so responsible AI needs diverse data, bias testing, human oversight and clear rules about how systems are used.
Data science combines statistics, programming and domain knowledge to extract insights from data. A typical workflow: collect, clean, explore, model, evaluate and communicate the results.

Python is the most popular language for AI thanks to its simple syntax and rich libraries: NumPy and pandas for data, scikit-learn for classic machine learning, NLTK and spaCy for NLP, and TensorFlow or PyTorch for deep learning.

Syntecxhub is a company that bridges learning with practical experience, offering internship projects in web development, UI/UX design, front-end and back-end development, data science, AI and more, with mentorship and hands-on tasks. Its motto is Create | Think | Solve.
